story: In Inuvialuktun, tuktut nogait means a young caribou, from the day it drops wobbly-legged onto the tundra until it is about a year old. The name is the park's reason for being. The community of Paulatuk proposed protecting the land for caribou in 1988, and the park takes in most of the core calving and post-calving grounds of the Bluenose West herd, which returns each June to calve; in years when its numbers are high, the Bluenose East herd uses the park after calving too.

The park represents the Tundra Hills natural region and lies wholly above the treeline, on continuous permafrost. Three rivers, the Hornaday, the Brock and the Roscoe, drain it north-west to Amundsen Gulf, and where they leave the uplands they have cut deep, sheer canyons into layers of shale, siltstone, dolomite and sandstone. The Hornaday is the largest, 360 kilometres long, peaking in the first week of June. The central Melville Hills are bare, with few lakes, but from late June to the end of July the tundra elsewhere is thick with lupine, moss campion, purple saxifrage and other flowers.

Wildlife gathers along the river corridors. Barren-ground grizzly bears are found throughout, with wolves, wolverines, red foxes, muskoxen and arctic ground squirrels. Peregrine falcons, gyrfalcons, rough-legged hawks and golden eagles nest on the canyon walls, and tundra swans, sandhill cranes, loons and golden plovers are among the birds that come to this major breeding ground. The rivers hold arctic char, grayling, lake trout and whitefish; the Hornaday's char are an important food for the people of Paulatuk.

People have lived here since about AD 1000, and more than 360 archaeological sites are known, from tent rings and caches to rock alignments, meat-drying areas and hunting blinds, the oldest probably Thule or Copper Inuit, the more recent Inuvialuit. Father Émile Petitot was the first European to reach the area, in 1867–68. A Catholic mission opened at Paulatuk in 1935, close to coal along the Hornaday. Under the Tuktut Nogait Agreement of 1996 the park was established by Parliament in 1998 and expanded south into the Délı̨nę District of the Sahtú Settlement Area in 2005. Inuvialuit and Sahtúgot'įne keep their harvesting rights here.
howItWorks: Every visitor must attend an orientation, register with Parks Canada and get a permit before entering the park, and de-register at the end. Book a time with the Parks Canada office in Inuvik and allow about an hour: staff go over hazards, route conditions, weather, water levels, closures, regulations and bear safety, and you give your group's contacts, emergency contacts, equipment, itinerary and de-registration date, and pay the Northern Park Backcountry Excursion/Camping fee. A Superintendent's order makes all entry and travel a restricted activity. Because search and rescue is limited, the canyons of the Hornaday River below Uyarsivik Lake, including La Roncière Falls, are closed to hikers and paddlers. Non-commercial paddling groups must carry a satellite communication device, and Parks Canada strongly recommends at least two boats.

Most visitors arrive by charter floatplane from Norman Wells or sometimes Inuvik. There are no airstrips: only water landings are allowed, at lakes including Uyarsivik (Cache), Canoe, Long, One Island, Seven Island, Akluk, the Brock headwater lakes and Hornaday Lake. A free Aircraft Landing Permit is issued when you register, and landing without one, or flying for a company without a National Parks Business Licence, is an offence. Parks Canada keeps a list of groups wanting to share charters. You can also walk in from Paulatuk along the Hornaday, or take a boat shuttle to the Darnley Bay coast; both cross private Inuvialuit lands, so contact the Inuvialuit Land Administration first. In winter, ski-planes can land, and snowmobiles may go only as far as the boundary.

Barren-ground grizzlies live throughout the park, most of all in the greener areas. Watch Parks Canada's Staying Safe in Bear Country film and read its grizzly bear brochure before you go, cook and store food carefully, travel in groups and make noise near streams and shrubby valley bottoms. Polar bears mostly stay on the pack ice but can be met along the coast when the ice is blown towards the mainland. Firearms are not allowed. In November 2026 Parks Canada listed the backcountry permit at $37 per person per night or $259 for a year, and a fishing permit at $22.25 a day.

sightNotes.poi-ca-tuktut-nogait-hornaday-river: The park's largest river, 360 kilometres from the upland tundra to Amundsen Gulf. Paddled in 8 to 12 days in July, starting at Hornaday Lake or on the main river.
sightNotes.poi-ca-tuktut-nogait-uyarsivik-cache-lak: Where most Hornaday paddling trips end, above the canyons. A floatplane landing lake, with a cabin and a set of Parks Canada's red chairs.
sightNotes.poi-ca-tuktut-nogait-la-ronciere-falls: A 21-metre waterfall in the last of the Hornaday's three canyon sections. The canyons below Uyarsivik Lake, falls included, are currently closed to visitors.
sightNotes.poi-ca-tuktut-nogait-seven-islands-lake: One of the lakes in the north-west of the park where floatplanes can land.

entrances: By charter floatplane from Norman Wells or sometimes Inuvik to a landing lake such as Uyarsivik (Cache), Canoe, Long, One Island, Seven Island, Akluk or Hornaday Lake
On foot from Paulatuk: the Hornaday delta is 15 kilometres by land from the hamlet, and the west bank leads about 40 kilometres to the park boundary
By boat shuttle from Paulatuk to the Darnley Bay coast near the Brock and Hornaday deltas, arranged through the Paulatuk Hunters and Trappers Committee
In winter by ski-equipped aircraft; snowmobiles only as far as the boundary
planYourVisit.reservations: Book an orientation and registration time with the Parks Canada office in Inuvik before you go. Book rooms and meals at the Paulatuk Hotel well in advance. Aklak Air's scheduled Inuvik–Paulatuk flights run on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Fridays, and schedules change — check before you go.
permits: Northern Park Backcountry Excursion/Camping Permit, issued at registration
Aircraft Landing Permit, free, issued at registration
National Park Fishing Permit, from the Parks Canada offices in Inuvik or Paulatuk; territorial licences are not valid
Permits for food or fuel caches, commercial filming and photography, and research
camping: No designated campsites: camp on durable ground anywhere except at archaeological sites; Parks Canada's Hornaday River Guide suggests sites
No campfires: cook on a stove, and buy fuel in Inuvik or Paulatuk, since scheduled flights will not carry it
Do not build cairns or inuksuit; scatter any rocks used to hold down tents
lodging: None in the park; the ten-room Paulatuk Hotel, and hotels in Inuvik and Norman Wells
seasonalClosures: The Hornaday canyons below Uyarsivik Lake, including La Roncière Falls, are closed to hiking and paddling — check with Parks Canada before you go
Winter-like conditions from October until May

chronology.text: People begin to occupy the land now in the park.
Father Émile Petitot becomes the first European to reach the area.
The Hudson's Bay Company opens a post at Letty Harbour; it closes in 1937.
A Roman Catholic mission is set up at Paulatuk, near coal along the Hornaday River.
Most people leave the Paulatuk mission for work at the DEW Line site being built at Cape Parry; they return to Paulatuk in the mid-1960s.
The community of Paulatuk proposes a park to protect the caribou calving grounds.
The Tuktut Nogait Agreement sets out the park and its cooperative management board.
Parliament formally establishes Tuktut Nogait National Park.
The park is expanded south into the Délı̨nę District of the Sahtú Settlement Area.

safety: Tuktut Nogait is one of the most isolated parks in North America. Search and rescue staff are based in Inuvik and shared with Ivvavik and Aulavik; carry advanced first-aid skills and satellite communications.
The Hornaday and Brock rivers are dangerous to cross after rain and during the spring melt. Cross only at low water, early in the day.
Box canyons flood fast in heavy rain or on hot days of snowmelt. Stay out of them then, keep away from undercut banks and overhangs, and take great care near waterfalls: there are no railings.
Giardiasis has been reported here. Filter, boil or treat all drinking water.
Compasses are unreliable in parts of the park and the open tundra is hard to navigate; carry a GPS and keep to landmarks such as rivers, canyons and eskers.
regulations: Register, attend the orientation and carry your permit; de-register when you leave.
No recreational drones: flying one can bring a fine of up to $25,000.
No campfires and no firearms; pets must be on a leash at all times.
Fishing only with a National Park Fishing Permit, and one fish a day.
Leave artefacts, bones, antlers and other natural objects where you find them.

weather: A low-Arctic climate of long, cold winters and short, cool summers: the mean temperature is 5°C in summer and -26°C in winter, and only 200 to 300 millimetres of precipitation falls in a year. The north is cooled by Amundsen Gulf and gets more fog and rain; the centre and south swing more widely. The sun stays up for almost two months in summer and does not rise for two months in winter, and the wind hardly ever stops. July is the most reliable month. Rain, icy winds, snow and frost can come even in midsummer, and sudden, heavy fog at any time in summer and early autumn. Wildflowers peak from late June, autumn colours in the third week of August.
directions: Inuvik has daily scheduled flights from southern Canada, and Aklak Air flies on from Inuvik to Paulatuk, the nearest community, about 420 kilometres to the east. Paulatuk, a hamlet of about 300 people 40 kilometres west of the park, has a hotel, a Northern Store with basic groceries and an ATM, a health centre and an RCMP detachment, and the Parks Canada office and Tuktut Nogait Interpretation Centre in the same building as the hotel and store. No road or trail leads from Paulatuk to the park. Norman Wells, with daily flights from Calgary, Edmonton, Yellowknife and Inuvik, is the other base for floatplane charters. Allow at least two spare days at each end of a trip for weather.
